lesson.menu_desc: A phone call with the debtor’s lawyer: offers, counteroffers and conditions -- If he pays a lump sum, we’ll waive the interest / unless / as long as -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 7 -- The Settlement Call
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Caroline Teixeira Nomiyama | Lesson 7 -- The Settlement Call
lesson.grammar_point: first conditional: if + present, will + verb (If he pays a lump sum, we will waive the interest); unless = if not (We will file a lawsuit unless he pays by Friday); as long as = only if (As long as he pays on time, we will not go to court); never will after if

listenings.text: I've worked as a mediator for twenty years, and here's something that surprises people. Most of the cases I see never reach a judge. They end in a settlement. Why? Because a lawsuit is slow and expensive. If you go to court, you'll probably wait two or three years, and you'll pay lawyers the whole time. And at the end, nobody knows the result. So both sides usually prefer a deal they can control. My advice is simple. Know your limit before the meeting starts. If you know the lowest number you'll accept, you won't panic when the other side makes an offer.

When a client can't pay, we don't go to court on the first day. First, we negotiate. Usually, we offer a payment plan in monthly installments. The rule is clear. As long as the client pays every installment on time, we won't add new fees. Some clients prefer to pay everything at once. If a client pays a lump sum, we'll waive part of the interest, because cash today is better for us than promises for a year. But the plan has one more rule. If the client defaults, the plan ends, and the full debt is due again. We explain this very clearly before anybody signs.

My first negotiations in English were a disaster. I understood the other lawyer, but I accepted the first offer too fast, because I wanted to finish the conversation. Now I prepare three sentences before every call. One to say no politely: I'm afraid that's too low. One for my counteroffer. And one for my condition, usually with unless or as long as. For example: we'll accept, as long as the first payment arrives this month. And if the other lawyer speaks too fast, I ask him to repeat the numbers, slowly. Numbers are the one thing you can never guess in a negotiation.
